title: A New Age of Sail
text:
Photographs by Peter Fisher 

 For a few hours , it was magical. The Neoliner Origin, the world’s largest sailing cargo ship, was cruising across the Atlantic Ocean powered by nothing but wind. Four huge sails billowed from masts towering 90 meters above the waterline. The ship had an engine, but it was shut off. The vessel, half again as long as a football field, sliced through the waters at nearly 16 knots, close to the speed of an engine-powered freighter. Earlier in the day, the ship had been burning 400 liters of marine diesel an hour. Now the only sounds were the waves slapping the hull below us and the wind rumbling through the sails above.

 This was something at once novel and ancient. People have been using sails to propel themselves for millennia. The ancient Egyptians, who developed linen sails, so closely associated wind with boats that their hieroglyphic sign for wind showed a hoisted sail. Polynesians traversed enormous expanses of the Pacific in canoes mounted with sails, navigating by the stars. Wind-powered navigation reached its zenith during what historians call the Age of Sail—the era of Columbus and Magellan, Hudson and Cook. The great ships of the time were square-rigged, using multiple masts and a combination of stacked rectangular sails, triangular jibs, and quadrilateral gaff sails. Empires were built on wind and canvas.

 But starting in 1807, when Robert Fulton launched his first paddle-wheel steamboat, sails were gradually relegated to museum ships, pleasure craft, and racing boats. Elegant clippers were replaced by hulking, engine-powered cargo carriers. These vessels make modern society possible, but they also endanger it. Most cargo ships run on heavy fuel oil—a thick, sulfurous residue left over from refining crude oil. Shipping produces 3 percent of global carbon emissions every year, according to the International Maritime Organization, a United Nations agency that regulates global shipping—more than all airplanes and about the same as all U.S. coal plants. The IMO has set a rough target date of 2050 for phasing out greenhouse-gas emissions from shipping completely.

 Many naval architects and shipping companies expect that new technologies, making use of hydrogen and ammonia as well as batteries, will one day replace oil, but despite years of research, none of these is yet up to the task. A small but growing group of designers and engineers has taken a different approach, betting that wind can be the energy source of the future—one that is free and renewable. “To me, it’s a complete no-brainer,” Gavin Allwright, who leads the International Windship Association, told me. “It’s like, please tell me why you wouldn’t want to be saving money.” More than 120 merchant ships now use some form of wind technology. Another 120 are on the way. China and Europe dominate the industry. (The rickety U.S. shipbuilding industry is not in the competition.)

 Neoline, the French company that operates the Neoliner Origin, is by no means the largest player in the quest for wind-powered cargo ships, but it might be the most ambitious. Where other shippers aim to reduce fuel consumption by 15 to 20 percent, Neoline aims to sail mostly with wind, cutting fuel consumption by as much as 80 percent compared with a conventional ship. It began cargo service in 2025, hauling Renault cars (as well as brioche and cognac) between France and North America. If its venture succeeds, Neoline could help usher in a new Age of Sail on the high seas.

 We had used wind only sparingly on our journey up the Eastern Seaboard. Stormy weather had often kept the sails stowed and the ship’s crew confined belowdecks. But now that we’d moved into the open sea, our world took on the aura of a Wes Anderson movie: oversaturated blue sky and bright sun accentuated by the absurdity of traveling on a sailboat the size of a destroyer. I had been invited aboard the Neoliner Origin for its third round trip between Saint-Nazaire, on France’s west coast, and the Port of Baltimore. After a stop at Saint‑Pierre, the main commercial port of Saint‑Pierre and Miquelon, a tiny French territory off the coast of Newfoundland, we were bound for Europe. The ship carried nine officers, mostly French; eight crew members, all West African; and a handful of passengers. Michel Péry, the chairman of Neoline, was also aboard—an avuncular retired captain with a pointy mustache, an imperturbable demeanor, and a stock of sea stories honed by retelling. Mechanical difficulties had marred the Neoliner Origin’s previous voyages, but now everything seemed to have come together. The coast of Brittany was just a week of fair winds away.

 Then, at 9:41 p.m., a day after we left Saint‑Pierre, a loud noise shook the ship.

 Unless you are an importer, a stevedore, or a seafarer, the shipping industry is all but invisible until something goes wrong. In 2020, the onset of COVID stranded ships around the world, snarling supply chains and leaving shelves empty. In 2021, the container ship Ever Given ran aground in the Suez Canal, bringing transit to a halt for six days. In 2024, the freighter Dali lost power and struck the Francis Scott Key Bridge , in Baltimore, killing six workers and cutting off both marine and highway traffic through a busy port.

 Last February, I stood at the rail of the Neoliner Origin as it sailed past the standing piers of that bridge and headed south down the Chesapeake Bay. Herman Melville captured the magnetic pull of the ocean in the opening pages of Moby‑Dick —“Why upon your first voyage as a passenger, did you yourself feel such a mystical vibration, when first told that you and your ship were now out of sight of land?”—but the endless plain of the sea eventually turns mystical vibration into something else. I gradually lost track of the days and, as we crossed time zones, the hours.

 At 136 meters, the Neoliner Origin is larger than most watercraft but smaller than most freighters. (The Titanic was 269 meters long; the world’s largest cargo ships now top out at 400.) It is a “roll-on, roll-off,” or Ro-Ro, ship, which means that instead of carrying huge stacks of metal containers, it is more like a car ferry, transporting vehicles or containers loaded on low trailers. With its sharp, vertical bow and its black-and-red hull, the ship evokes the great ocean liners of the 20th century.

 Unlike an old-fashioned tall ship, which has four or five masts and dozens of canvas sails, the Neoliner Origin has just two masts and four sails. The masts, which are made of carbon and weigh 20 tons each, can fold down to allow the ship to pass under bridges. When they are raised to full height, they look like twin sailboats perched on the ship’s deck.

 Each mast rises from a broad, horizontal metal boom, called a balestron , that can rotate 360 degrees to let the sails catch the wind. On one side of the mast is a rigid mainsail, comprising 10 hard quadrilateral panels and one hard triangle on top. The panels, made from carbon fiber and fiberglass, fold like an accordion when not in use. On the other side is a jib, closer to the conventional idea of a sail: a huge fabric triangle connected to the mast and to a diagonal stay on the hypotenuse. Together, the sails cover 3,000 square meters, about three-quarters of an acre. They can be hoisted and lowered, furled and unfurled, from the ship’s bridge, or controlled from a console within the balestrons, which swivel silently when the officer steering the ship adjusts them and are large enough to stand inside. Once, I was inside a balestron when it began to rotate, and I didn’t even notice it was moving.

 An unusual ship attracts an unusual type of mariner. Captain Magaly Dupuy Denat told me she’d been following Neoline’s progress for a decade before she sailed on the ship. Female captains remain rare in the merchant marine. Dupuy Denat and her husband, Chief Engineer Paul Pélaprat, had even invested in Neoline. Pélaprat has been working at sea for more than 20 years, but had “always dreamed of being on a cargo ship, sailing,” he told me. He sometimes wore a T-shirt that read MARINE ENGINEER: I SOLVE PROBLEMS YOU DON’T KNOW YOU HAVE IN WAYS YOU CAN’T UNDERSTAND . Samuel Veaute, the ship’s young sail mate, had come aboard after quitting a job on a five-masted Mediterranean cruise ship in order to take a month-long solo transatlantic voyage in his small sailboat. Now Veaute spent much of each day in a harness, outside among his sails, ascending and descending with childlike delight no matter how miserable the conditions aloft. “Maybe I read too much books of sailors,” he told me with a shrug.

 Peter Fisher for The Atlantic 

 Captain Magaly Dupuy Denat on the bridge

 Peter Fisher for The Atlantic 

 Sail Mate Samuel Veaute repairs one of the Neoliner Origin’s mainsails. 

 The crew’s life is sometimes monotonous, but it is never idle. Some tasks are common to any ship. Every officer has to sit watch for two four-hour shifts each day. Safety equipment must be checked regularly. The boatswain is perpetually repainting to ward off rust. Seaports are full of peeling warehouses, rust-bucket boats, and grimy equipment. The Neoliner Origin stands out not only because of its masts and vertical bow but also because it still gleams with sharp lines and fresh paint, like a postmodern exhibition space. The huge cargo holds are immaculate. Even the engine room is spotless.

 But the Neoliner Origin presents special challenges. During its maiden voyage, in 2025, its aft mainsail cracked, disrupting the ship’s schedule and requiring a round trip using mostly engine power. By the time I was aboard, the mainsail had been repaired, but the motor that unfurled the aft jib was now broken—a replacement part was waiting at Saint‑Pierre. The balestrons were also balky. They are supposed to be fully automated and controllable from the bridge, but two engineers were on board to try to work out kinks in the software. Four nights out of Baltimore, the storm hit. I woke in the darkness to the sound of cabin furniture hurtling back and forth. The next day, one of the engineers had to lash his chair to a desk on the bridge so he could continue programming.

 Despite the 11 screens and dozens of electronic instruments on the bridge, many things have not changed since Melville went to sea. Although the Neoliner Origin’s 16-cylinder engine and electric motor meant we were never at risk of being adrift for days, I became attuned to the speed and direction of the wind. The ship of course had anemometers, but more than once, I watched officers head outside to put a finger in the air. Crew members still spent a great deal of time tying knots and stowing lines, but their harnesses and DayGlo jackets showed that safety standards had improved since the days when barefoot tars clambered up masts.

 The Neoliner Origin is effectively a $78 million prototype. Aviation-inspired rigid sails have become a staple in sport racing—for instance, in the America’s Cup —and the balestron system has been used on smaller sailboats. But the Neoliner Origin is the first ship to use a version this size at sea. (The balestrons’ builder, the French shipyard Chantiers de l’Atlantique, has since constructed a three-masted luxury cruiser using the same system.) Officers at the helm can consult a matrix of recommended sail alignments for any given wind speed and direction, but figuring out what actually works is a matter of trial and error. “Nobody has experience in this,” Pélaprat said.

 Nevertheless, the engineering headaches gave way to wonder on the deck when all four sails were full of wind. Queasy passengers and salt-hardened mariners alike craned their necks upward. This first moment purely under wind power was the only time when all other activity on the ship seemed to pause. Eventually, everyone dispersed, but we’d find ourselves drawn back to the deck to gawk, still somewhat disbelieving that a 12,000-ton ship was being propelled by nothing but the breeze.

 Peter Fisher for The Atlantic 

 The Neoliner Origin, bound for France, departs Saint-Pierre and Miquelon, a French territory off the coast of Newfoundland.

 Sailing with the wind at your back is straightforward. Sailing into the wind is more complex: It is achieved by tacking—sailing at an angle to the wind. Problems arise when there is no wind at all. Although wind is cheap everywhere, it is not plentiful everywhere. Renewed interest in wind propulsion has spawned research, nearly incomprehensible to nonspecialists, that seeks to calculate the most efficient routes for wind-powered ships, which sometimes involves covering more total distance in order to find wind than a direct route would have entailed. As in the past, sail-powered ships take advantage of winds that rotate clockwise around the Atlantic, pushing south from Europe, westward across the tropical Atlantic and Caribbean, up the East Coast, and then back across to Europe. The Neoliner Origin’s course carried it approximately 250 miles north of where the Titanic sank. At that latitude, we saw few other ships. When we finally encountered one, the officer on watch was eager to know what the Neoliner Origin looked like at sea with its sails up. Like a tourist, he asked his counterpart on the passing ship to take a picture and text it to him.

 A strong wind exerts enormous force against a sail. Too much wind can be as bad as too little. Wind is also fickle: Changing winds helped the reeling Spanish Armada escape Queen Elizabeth’s navy, but then dashed many of the surviving galleons against Ireland’s Atlantic coast. Wind is calibrated according to the Beaufort scale , an unexpectedly poetic name for a form of measurement. At 25 miles an hour—what the Beaufort scale calls a “strong breeze”—a direct wind would put nearly 30 tons of pressure on the four sails of the Neoliner. At 40 miles an hour, the force of the wind against the sails would be equivalent to the thrust of an Airbus A330’s engines.

 The loud sound we’d heard at 9:41 p.m. was wind breaking sail. As the crew soon discovered, three of the huge carbon-fiber panels on the fore mainsail had cracked under the force of the wind. The balestron had been tested on land before being installed on the ship, but simulating the actual stresses at sea was difficult, and although the aft mainsail had been reinforced after breaking on the Neoliner’s first journey, the foresail hadn’t been upgraded yet. Now it would have to be stowed for the rest of the crossing.

 The mood at breakfast the next morning was gloomy and at one point turned to superstition. Michel Péry, Neoline’s chairman, even thought to bring up, with artful indirection, a bit of hoary lore—the injunction against saying rabbit aboard a ship, although who might have uttered the word was unclear. Just then, another sound boomed through the Neoliner. Rushing onto the deck, we saw that the top panel of the intact aft mainsail had broken free of the rail on which it slid up the mast. It was now flapping dangerously in the wind. Half a dozen officers and engineers in harnesses and hard hats mounted the balestron to lower it. After several attempts failed, Pélaprat, a rock climber, shimmied up the mast and lassoed the panel with a line to secure it.

 The mood now turned from gloomy to black. One officer, garrulous in normal circumstances, moped melodramatically throughout his evening watch. With the mainsails out of commission, he had no option but to set a course, run the engine, and put autopilot in charge. In a self-mocking tone, he announced, “There is nothing left to break but my heart.”

 Peter Fisher for The Atlantic 

 Each of the ship’s two masts, towering 90 meters above the waterline, supports a fabric jib and a rigid mainsail.

 Péry himself was uncharacteristically somber. When I asked what he was feeling, he replied, “Doubt.” He had been dreaming of something like the Neoliner for almost 20 years. From his youth in the Pays Basque, in France’s southwest, Péry seemed destined for a maritime career. One grandfather, a shipwright, built the ships that the other grandfather sailed. His father was a mariner too. Péry followed them to sea on Ro-Ro ships around the world. At the start of his career, sailors had barely more idea what kinds of conditions they’d encounter than their forebears had centuries ago. For nearly four decades, he watched fuzzy, inscrutable forecasts give way to fine-grained, real-time updates that let him choose safer courses. Péry also spent many years as skipper of the Belem, a historic French tall ship .

 Motivated by climate change, Péry wondered whether he could combine his experience on the Belem with advances in forecasting to create a modern version of the old sailing cargo ships. By 2023, Péry and a group of partners had secured money to build a ship in a Turkish shipyard. Its dimensions were modeled on the France II, a barque launched in 1911—one of the largest merchant sailing ships ever built, and one of the last of that age.

 By then, others were also experimenting with wind. Most shippers who have adopted wind seek to supplement rather than supplant engine power. One popular approach is the use of rotor sails, which look like tall pillars erected on the deck of a ship, usually alone or in groups. In the 1920s, the German engineer Anton Flettner showed that a spinning column could produce lift, lowering the speed of air on one side and increasing it on the other. He mounted his rotors on two ships , but cheap fossil fuel rendered them superfluous for nearly a century. Now a company called Norsepower, based in Finland, makes rotor sails from high-tech composites that significantly cut fuel consumption. Norsepower has installed rotor sails on 31 vessels, and 28 more orders are on its books.

 Another approach is a suction sail, which looks similar but generates additional lift by drawing air in and blowing it out the top with an electric fan to increase lift. Some ships are experimenting with rigid “wing sails,” akin to airplane wings mounted vertically, which can reduce fuel consumption by about a third. Others are using kites—large pieces of fabric tethered to a ship by cable—to catch wind.

 Not all vessels are equally suited to wind propulsion. The most adaptable ships are those with flat decks, including the huge ships that haul cars in their holds across oceans. Ironically, oil tankers are very well suited to wind. Container ships, which carry many consumer goods, are trickier because their decks are piled high with metal boxes. In 2027, the Danish shipping giant Maersk will become the first operator to test a rotor sail on a container ship.

 Given that the global merchant fleet encompasses tens of thousands of ships, there’s plenty of opportunity to test a range of designs, and for more than one to succeed. Perhaps because the potential market is so large, wind-propulsion companies seem to maintain cordial relationships. Captain Dupuy Denat told me she viewed other wind entrepreneurs more as comrades than as competitors. “Even if it’s not Neoliner Origin,” she said, “what we want is to see thousands and thousands of cargo sailing ships.”

 Peter Fisher for The Atlantic 

 East of Nova Scotia, a storm overtakes the ship. 

 In rough seas, the rolling of a ship from side to side can be disconcerting, but you learn to appreciate its predictability. A ship that pops back up to center too quickly will shake cargo loose, sicken its crew, and risk capsizing. A well-balanced ship achieves a smooth equilibrium. Within 36 hours of the damage to the mainsails, the mood aboard the Neoliner Origin had also righted itself. The sails could be repaired in France, and by slowing the engine and sailing with jibs, we could arrive in Saint-Nazaire only slightly behind schedule and without burning too much diesel. Fuel was on everyone’s mind: While we were at sea, the U.S. and Israeli governments had launched a war against Iran, and marine-diesel prices were rising . Donald Trump’s tariffs had already made it harder for Neoline to fill the cargo hold with French goods bound for the United States and to sign up new customers. Now he was making it harder to fill the fuel bunkers, too.

 But Trump can’t be blamed for wind gusts. Although modern technology allows mariners to see storms coming, gusts—sudden, brief bursts of wind—defy easy detection. They are the ghosts in the weather machine, mysterious and malign. The most powerful recorded gust, outside of tropical cyclones, was 231 miles an hour (in 1934, in New Hampshire), and more typical ones can topple trees and upend buildings. Climate change has altered wind patterns and airflow, leading to an increase in violent turbulence that has disrupted air travel. Péry told me he’d experienced more capricious gusts in the North Atlantic as well.

 Shortly after midnight on March 5, six days after we’d lost the fore mainsail, another sharp crack resounded through the ship. A gust had kicked up, too fast for the officer on watch to furl the jib or turn the balestron to a safer angle. The balestron had been designed to let the line go slack if the load on the sail became too great, but the auto-release mechanism had failed, and the huge stainless-steel ring that connected the bottom of the aft jib to the mast broke free, leaving the fabric flapping pathetically. We were down to one usable sail, the fore jib.

 The jib’s failure illustrated another challenge of outfitting a sailing cargo ship. The only sails and winches large enough for the Neoliner Origin are designed for the biggest luxury yachts, but equipment meant to be used a few days a year on an oligarch’s plaything may not be up to the demands of year-round North Atlantic crossings. A new Age of Sail will also require merchants and consumers to accept trade-offs. Just-in-time logistics—the modern practice of getting raw materials and finished goods to customers at the last minute to save on the cost of storage—assumes speedy and predictable delivery, but even with wind routing and favorable itineraries, wind-powered ships can’t usually move as fast as fuel-burning vessels at top speed.

 Gavin Allwright, the wind-ship advocate, sees the fair-trade movement as proof that consumers will pay higher prices for goods that are less destructive to workers and the environment. He hopes that people will be willing to receive goods a few days later in exchange for a lower carbon footprint. But although fair trade is commercially viable, it’s a niche market, dwarfed by the instant gratification that Amazon Prime offers. A French company called TOWT had some success carrying alcohol on smaller, traditional wind-powered ships starting in 2011, but it declared bankruptcy this past spring.

 To significantly reduce emissions, wind must be more than a boutique service. Despite the growing number of wind ships, the major shipping companies that operate most of the world’s fleet remain cautious. Some large shippers have committed to goals of net-zero emissions by 2040 or 2050, but the pledges are not binding.

 Regulation would be more meaningful. The European Union has introduced carbon pricing for ships that travel to or from the bloc, but the International Maritime Organization—the only body that can affect the whole planet—is dominated by shipping interests . The IMO has struggled to enact guidelines for hitting its 2050 net-zero target. Members were expected to adopt a plan in 2025, but negotiations foundered when the U.S. delegation threatened to retaliate against countries that signed on.

 A painting in the Neoliner Origin’s passenger lounge imagines the vessel as heir to a lineage that includes the Egyptian felucca, the Viking longship, and the Chinese junk. Now, after the jib failure, one of the officers joked that the ship reminded him of The Raft of the Medusa . We would motor the rest of the way to Saint-Nazaire, occasionally flying the surviving jib for a boost.

 Slow progress is the rule, not the exception, in transportation. No steamship was able to cross the Atlantic fully under steam until more than three decades after Robert Fulton’s first voyage. More than four decades passed between the Wright brothers’ first flight at Kitty Hawk and the start of large-scale commercial aviation. And progress is sometimes found by looking backwards. It’s easy to forget that some of the world’s first automobiles were electric.

 At the quay in Saint-Nazaire, the crew was thinking about the present, not the past. By the time passengers were allowed to disembark, climbers had boarded the ship, scaled the mast, and freed the torn jib so it could be replaced. A plan had been set to move the surviving rigid sail from the aft mast to the fore, maximizing wind power while its twin was repaired onshore. A fresh captain and chief engineer would take over for the next rotation, so Dupuy Denat hurried through preparations to hand off command. Within a few days, the ship would head back out to the North Atlantic, laden with cargo and searching for favorable winds.
